Can girls-only fests close techs gender gap?

This is something I think about a lot. I'm of two minds about it.

While the number of girls-only Stem initiatives are on the rise, one wonders whether such events might inadvertently state the gender gap more strongly by separating the girls from the boys. Is the exclusion of males really necessary for the creation of sisterhood? In the end, it comes down to giving girls the chance to have their voice heard in a secure environment – and one, as Saujani puts it, that is deliberately miles away from the stereotype of “geeky guys locked in dark basements”. By giving girls the chance to collaborate on their own terms, they can change the culture around them.

On the one hand, many boys DO grow up with exactly this segregated environment. The status quo isn't getting any more girls involved, so opportunities like this can help with that.

On the other hand, what comes from segregation is an inability to work together - and this is true on both sides. On the job is not the place to figure out how to work together with people of the opposite sex.

All of this work is going into pushing girls into STEP while ignoring the fact that the ones that do get into (specifically tech) aren't sticking around. The only company who seems to be interested in working on this (at least publicly) is Google.

When it comes to kids, what the movement is/should be fighting is the culture in which parents are discouraging their daughters from getting involved in this stuff, or girls just don't choose to get involved with the same stuff as the boys are. I'm not disparaging parents, here. I do believe it's mostly a million unconscious things throughout their lives which show girls that they'll be looked down upon for getting involved in STEM. From there, make opportunities for a wide variety of kids. Kids are perfectly capable of working together, and this would include other underrepresented groups. Ever met a Native American coder?
Did you know that girls are different than boys, and tend to like different things?

Yup! I also know that girls are subtly shifted away from science stuff by friends and family who don't even realize they're doing it.

Not all girls will be interested in science and math. Not all boys will be, either.

One of the things these programs are trying to address is that girls tend to have less exposure to this stuff at a young age, and almost no exposure to female professionals in STEM that they can look up to.

I've always been interested in this. In my part of the world everyone is encouraged to get into STEM. If you go another way then there's no issue. There appears to be a cultural bias in the West which I have never noticed over here.

A lot of the highest achievers in my Physics, Math, Chem or early Bio classes were all girls. The gap between the boys and girls only closed in the 9th, 10th, 11th and 12th grades.

Don't take this to mean anymore than my pure anecdotal evidence but it has interested me.

Yup, me, too.

At this point we have no idea how much of this kind of preference is cultural and how much is really based on gender. You can't do a study where you separate children from their own culture!
